# Results — Study 38 (Chorus) on the real S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily total-return panel of the **current
S&P 500** (263 names with ≥2500 days of history) via the shared `quantlab.universe` engine, 2010–2026. We
build three simple, causal, dollar-neutral cross-sectional signals — **momentum** (12-1 month
winners-minus-losers, Study 24), **reversal** (5-day contrarian fade, Study 33) and a **low-vol** tilt
(long the low-realised-vol names) — each normalised to gross exposure 1, then combine them into one book
both **equal-weight** and **inverse-vol (risk-parity)**. The offline core proves the apparatus on a
synthetic panel carrying three weak, decorrelated components; this is the measurement on the market.
As-of **2026-06-10** (the cache ends 2026-06-05); match the fingerprint below. **Caveat:** the panel is
today's index membership → survivorship bias; the qualitative combo-vs-parts result is robust, exact
magnitudes are not.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · Whole > parts? `MIXED`

The alpha-combo thesis (Kakushadze-Serur §3.20; the Fundamental Law, Grinold-Kahn) is that **several weak,
decorrelated signals blend into a portfolio stronger than any component** — Sharpe ≈ IC · √breadth. On the
synthetic control where every component carries a real, independent edge, that is exactly what happens:
three thin signals (Sharpe 1.5 / 2.1 / 1.2) combine to **2.71**, above every soloist, with average
pairwise correlation **+0.02**. On the real S&P 500 the *mechanism* is plainly visible but its *promise*
is only half-kept. The three components are genuinely decorrelated (average pairwise correlation
**−0.03**), and the **momentum + reversal** pair does the textbook thing — gross Sharpe **0.66**, above
both its parts (0.36 and 0.64). But the third voice is off-key: the low-vol tilt earns **−0.89** on this
current-membership panel over a high-beta-led bull market, and dropping it into the chorus drags the naive
3-signal equal-weight combo to a flat **0.00** gross. The lesson is sharper than the slogan: **breadth
helps only when each added bet has positive expectancy** — a decorrelated *loser* doesn't diversify, it
dilutes. And net of even 1 bp the whole thing is gone: turnover **0.38/day**, **break-even 0.02 bp** — a
textbook `MIRAGE` to trade.

## Data stamp

- **Panel**: 263 S&P 500 names, 2010-01-05 → 2026-06-05, 4130 days, inputs fingerprint `9b06cd44bb81`
- **As-of**: 2026-06-10 (cache ends 2026-06-05)
- **Caveat**: current-membership panel ⇒ survivorship bias (delisted names absent), and the low-vol
  anomaly is the most survivorship-sensitive of the three.

## Standalone components vs the combo (GROSS)

| book | Sharpe | CAGR | vol | turnover/day |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| momentum (12-1) | +0.36 | +2.8% | 8.6% | 0.09 |
| reversal (5-day) | +0.64 | +4.9% | 7.9% | 0.63 |
| low-vol | **−0.89** | −8.7% | 9.7% | 0.05 |
| **COMBO (equal-wt)** | **+0.00** | −0.3% | 7.7% | 0.38 |
| COMBO (risk-parity) | −0.15 | −1.4% | 7.4% | 0.48 |

Two of three components are positive; the low-vol tilt inverts on this sample (high-beta names led the
2010–2026 rally), and because it is a *real, decorrelated* component the naive blend dutifully gives it
1/3 of the risk budget — sinking the chorus. Inverse-vol weighting doesn't rescue it: low-vol is the
*lowest*-turnover, middling-vol signal, so risk-parity actually *over*-weights it relative to its (poor)
information, leaving the risk-parity combo (−0.15) slightly *worse* than equal-weight (0.00). The clever
blend is not the lever; the *component roster* is.

## Whole > parts — `MIXED`: confirmed for the right pair, not for the naive chorus

| equal-weight blend | gross Sharpe |
|---|---|
| momentum + reversal | **+0.66** (> both parts: 0.36, 0.64) |
| momentum + low-vol | −0.37 |
| reversal + low-vol | −0.29 |

The diversification premium is *real and visible* — the momentum+reversal pair beats each of its
components, on a −0.03-correlated pair, exactly as the Fundamental Law predicts. But "throw all the
signals in and let breadth do the work" is **not** supported: a decorrelated component with negative
expectancy diversifies you straight into its loss. Breadth × IC needs the IC to be positive on every
voice.

## The breadth sweep — the Law works only over good bets

| # signals | components | gross Sharpe |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | momentum | +0.36 |
| 2 | momentum, reversal | +0.66 |
| 3 | momentum, reversal, low-vol | +0.00 |

Sharpe rises 1 → 2 signals (the √breadth lift), then collapses when the toxic third is added. On the
synthetic control (where all three carry real edge) the same sweep rises monotonically 1.49 → 2.57 →
2.71 — proof the apparatus captures the breadth effect when the components deserve it.

## The cost wall — `MIRAGE`

| cost (bp/unit) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 5 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| net Sharpe (equal-wt combo) | 0.002 | −0.121 | −0.244 | −0.614 | −1.229 |

The combo turns over **0.38 of its book per day** (it inherits the reversal leg's churn), so the
**break-even cost is 0.02 bp** — net-negative the instant any realistic cost is charged. Even the *healthy*
momentum+reversal pair (gross 0.66, net @1 bp 0.51) is thin once you account for survivorship and the
turnover it demands. The diversification edge is a measurement, not a trade.
